title: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31  - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief finds developed-country multi-year public climate-finance pledges have fallen ~70% (to about $11.7bn a year from around $40bn) as most pledges expired in 2025, with only the UK among major donors renewing while the US, Germany, France, Japan and COP31 co-host Australia have not. Aid cuts, defence spending, fiscal strain and far-right politics are blamed, making finance the key fault line at COP31 (the article mixes £ and $ labels for some headline totals).

themes.theme: Collapse in multi-year public climate-finance pledges

insights.claim: Carbon Brief analysis of the NRDC/E3G commitments tracker finds that pledged public climate finance from developed countries has fallen by about 71%, from roughly 42bn a year pre-2026 to about 11.8bn a year on average over the rest of the 2020s (the headline figures are given as $40bn falling to $11.7bn).
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A ~70% drop in pledged bilateral public climate finance signals a sharp contraction in a key funding stream for developing-country clean-energy and adaptation projects.
insights.locator: Carbon Brief analysis of this data

insights.claim: Nearly all developed-country multi-year climate-finance pledges expired in 2025, and only five nations have announced new multi-year pledges covering the period to 2030, with the UK the only major donor among them.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Pipeline visibility for concessional climate funding beyond 2025 is largely absent, raising financing risk for projects reliant on bilateral aid.
insights.locator: Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025

insights.claim: Bilateral public climate finance reached 43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount developed countries had pledged, implying recent delivery tracked pledges before the pledge cliff.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Past pledges were a reasonable predictor of actual flows, so the collapse in new pledges is a credible leading indicator of lower future flows.
insights.locator: While official data for 2025 is not yet available

insights.claim: Direct public spending from developed-country budgets, mainly foreign aid, has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years, alongside multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and mobilised private finance.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A shrinking bilateral aid channel puts more weight on MDBs and private mobilisation to fill the climate-finance gap.
insights.locator: But a large chunk is also expected

insights.claim: Developed countries agreed two years ago to take the lead on scaling annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035, a goal now at odds with the sharp fall in new public pledges.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The gap between the $300bn-by-2035 target and falling pledges is a source of negotiating friction and reliance on non-public finance sources.
insights.locator: The EU, the US and others agreed

insights.claim: The UK is the only one of the five dominant climate-finance donors (Japan, Germany, France, the US, the UK) to make a new pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29 plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget, accounting for half of all annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The UK is now the anchor bilateral donor; its accounting choices disproportionately shape headline pledge totals.
insights.locator: Of these key players, only the UK

insights.claim: The UK's new climate-finance pledge only appears more ambitious because the government changed its counting to include $8.9bn of 'additional' public finance such as equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit; on a like-for-like aid basis it is a drop in ambition.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Headline pledge growth can mask real cuts in grant-based aid; investors in climate-linked development finance should look at instrument mix, not totals.
insights.quote: When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the new pledge amounts to a drop in ambition.
insights.locator: The UK’s pledge appears more ambitious

insights.claim: The European Commission's average annual climate-finance contribution of $4.5bn to 2027 stems from an existing €28bn ($31.8bn) 2021-2027 budget promise rather than a new pledge, and its post-2027 contribution depends on ongoing EU budget negotiations.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Watch the next EU multiannual budget negotiation as the key determinant of post-2027 European climate-finance flows.
insights.locator: The European Commission makes up most of the remainder

insights.claim: Canada has pledged CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) of climate finance by 2030, averaging $860m a year, while the Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have pledged relatively small sums; overall new pledges are either less ambitious or only slightly more ambitious than previous ones.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: No donor is materially scaling up, contradicting the collective commitment to increase climate finance.
insights.locator: Canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn

insights.claim: The Dutch government says it will provide 'at least' €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually to 2031, while signalling total public climate finance will be considerably higher in 2026 and 2027.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Some donors may keep funds flowing without formal pledges, so pledge trackers may understate near-term flows.
insights.locator: The Dutch government, for example

insights.claim: The US, which committed under the Biden administration to reach $11.4bn in annual climate finance by 2024, has under Donald Trump withdrawn from the Paris Agreement for a second time, shrunk its aid budget, and will provide no official climate finance in coming years.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The single largest missing contribution removes an $11bn-scale annual flow from the global climate-finance pool.
insights.locator: The most significant absence is the US

insights.claim: Japan, the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, has not announced any new multi-year pledges and historically set goals bundling in private 'mobilised' finance rather than public-finance targets.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Japan's next climate-finance announcement is a key swing factor for total flows to developing countries.
insights.locator: Japan is the largest overall contributor

insights.claim: Australia, co-host of COP31 with Turkey, has not announced a climate-finance pledge, which Oxfam Australia warns would send a problematic message to those resisting climate action if it fails to do so as president of negotiations.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A host-country pledge (or its absence) is a near-term signal of COP31 negotiating momentum.
insights.quote: If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message
insights.locator: Another notable absence is Australia

themes.theme: European aid cuts and political shift

insights.claim: European governments, which provide the majority of international climate finance, have massively cut aid spending in recent years citing economic strain and defence spending needs.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Defence reprioritisation in Europe is directly crowding out climate aid budgets — a structural, not cyclical, headwind.
insights.locator: Europe provides the majority

insights.claim: Germany and France each pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) a year of climate finance by 2025 but have committed to nothing beyond that, and Germany missed its 2025 goal due to aid budget cuts.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Two of the largest European donors are absent from post-2025 pledges, deepening the funding gap.
insights.locator: Germany and France, the two largest

insights.claim: Experts say global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new climate funds, with Germany's CDU-led coalition deprioritising climate and France's upcoming presidential election and far-right influence complicating new commitments.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Political risk in key European donor countries points to persistently low public climate-finance pledges.
insights.quote: The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make new international financial commitments politically more difficult.
insights.locator: There has also been a political shift in France

insights.claim: Spain's snap election set for end of November and Sweden's ongoing coalition formation make new climate-finance pledges from those donors less likely during COP31.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Expect few, if any, new European pledges to emerge at COP31.
insights.locator: Other significant European donors

insights.claim: Developing countries are championing a 'climate-finance work programme' at COP31 to create space to discuss scaling up public climate finance, while the EU counters that its member states are the largest providers, citing a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025, and demands overdue emissions plans.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Finance is set to be the central fault line at COP31, risking slower progress on other negotiating tracks.
insights.locator: To highlight the lack of new pledges

insights.claim: EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra told Bloomberg that any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water, signalling the EU will not bring new climate funds to the table.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: An explicit EU no-new-money stance lowers odds of a COP31 finance breakthrough.
insights.quote: any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water
insights.locator: Against this backdrop, EU climate chief

insights.claim: NRDC's Joe Thwaites argues the lack of new pledge announcements is making finance negotiations tougher than needed because developing countries lack clarity on future public climate-finance volumes.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Low pledge visibility is a direct driver of negotiating gridlock and of developing-country demands for a dedicated work programme.
insights.quote: The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be.
insights.locator: Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director

insights.claim: The analysis covers 23 obligated developed countries plus the EU, excludes Japan and Norway for lacking specific public-finance pledges, and excludes Tropical Forest Forever Facility pledges, which would only shift the reduction from 71% to 70%.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The headline decline is robust to the inclusion of TFFF pledges, though omission of Japan means total flows could differ from pledge totals.
insights.locator: Methodology
